items.question: A defence maintenance provider runs a four-level agent hierarchy for fleet-readiness reporting: a root agent, three regional coordinator agents, and nine depot agents. The coordinators make no decisions — each forwards the root's brief to its depots and concatenates and shortens their returns. Engineers report that findings arriving at the root have lost the specifics needed to raise a work order, and cost per report is high. What should the architect change?

options.A: Remove the coordinator layer and have the root delegate directly to the nine depots, adding a middle layer back only if it owns a decision.
options.B: Keep the coordinators but instruct them to relay depot returns verbatim, so no operationally important detail is lost on the way up to the root.
options.C: Move the coordinators to a higher-capability tier so their shortening preserves the part numbers and fault codes a work order needs.
options.D: Add a validation layer beneath the depots that checks each depot's findings against the maintenance log before they pass upward.

items.question: A SaaS provider's incident-response system delegates root-cause investigation to a diagnostic subagent. When the subagent returns "cause not determined", the orchestrator re-delegates with the identical brief, up to three times. Traces show all three attempts following the same path to the same dead end, tripling the time to a human escalation during live incidents. The subagent's tooling and the underlying data are working correctly. What should change?

options.A: Increase the retry count from three to six so the investigation eventually diverges onto a different path.
options.B: Raise the subagent's sampling temperature on each successive retry so the attempts explore different hypotheses.
options.C: Escalate to a human responder on the first inconclusive return, since retrying an inconclusive investigation adds no new information.
options.D: Include prior attempts in the retry brief — hypotheses tested and what each ruled out — so the next starts where the last stopped.

items.question: Which THREE statements are true of the isolation between an orchestrator and a subagent it invokes? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The subagent inherits the caller's tool allowlist at invocation unless the handoff explicitly overrides it with a narrower set.
options.B: Material the subagent read is unavailable to the caller unless it was deliberately returned or persisted somewhere the caller can reach.
options.C: Constraints the caller established earlier in its conversation are invisible to the subagent unless the handoff carries them.
options.D: Caller and subagent draw on a single shared context window, so a long branch reduces the caller's remaining headroom.
options.E: An instruction embedded in content the subagent read can influence the caller only if it reaches the caller through the returned result.

items.question: An online travel agency's refund assistant delegates to a subagent that reads and summarises customer-submitted review text for a property. The summary is appended into the orchestrator's context. A review containing text addressed to the assistant caused the orchestrator to skip its usual eligibility check and recommend a full refund. The summarisation step must stay. What is the correct change?

options.A: Instruct the subagent to strip imperative sentences and any text addressed to an assistant from the review before it summarises the rest.
options.B: Place the summary in the orchestrator's system prompt, above the task instructions, so its provenance is unambiguous.
options.C: Validate the return against its schema, render it in a delimited block marked untrusted, and enforce eligibility outside the model.
options.D: Add a line to the orchestrator's prompt telling it to ignore any instructions that appear inside subagent returns or review text.

items.question: A patent office runs an agent that performs prior-art searches across several classification areas, with a per-request token budget set by the operations team. When the budget runs out mid-run, the agent returns whatever it has assembled, formatted exactly like a completed search. Examiners have twice issued opinions on searches that had covered only part of the classification set, believing them complete. Budgets cannot be raised globally. What should the design do on exhaustion?

options.A: Automatically extend the budget by a fixed 20% margin when exhaustion is detected mid-run, so most searches run to completion.
options.B: Return a distinct incomplete status naming the areas covered and those not reached, with the state needed to resume the search.
options.C: Discard the partial work and return a hard error to the examiner, so an incomplete search can never be mistaken for a complete one.
options.D: Append a sentence to the end of the returned search noting that coverage of the classification set may be incomplete.

items.question: What does threading a single correlation identifier through every handoff, tool call and artefact of a multi-agent request give the operator?

options.A: The ability to reassemble every branch's calls, returns and artefacts into a single trace for debugging.
options.B: Automatic deduplication of repeated state-changing calls made by branches that were retried after a timeout.
options.C: An enforced upper bound on how deep the delegation tree may go before further spawning is refused.
options.D: Shared reuse of a single cached prompt prefix across every agent taking part in the request.

items.question: A hotel group's concierge system was built quickly: each subagent's system prompt is a copy of the orchestrator's, with one task line appended. In production the subagents open with the orchestrator's guest greeting, attempt to plan and delegate work of their own, and on occasion address the guest directly in text that reaches the transcript. Guests receive replies that read as though several assistants are talking. What is the correct remedy?

options.A: Append a paragraph to the shared prompt stating that when acting as a subagent the model must not greet, plan or delegate work.
options.B: Remove only the persona and greeting sections from the copied prompt, keeping the shared operating instructions so behaviour stays consistent across agents.
options.C: Reduce each subagent's `max_tokens` allowance so there is no room for greetings or planning text before its result.
options.D: Give each agent a minimal prompt holding only its objective, output contract and tools, leaving guest-facing instructions with the orchestrator.

items.question: A hospital group's discharge-planning system fans out to subagents that each query the electronic health record. During ward rounds, many requests overlap and the EHR team reports that the assistant's traffic is degrading clinical users' response times. The EHR cannot be scaled. Which TWO controls belong in the orchestration layer? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A ceiling on the number of subagent branches in flight at once, applied per request and across the whole service.
options.B: A higher retry count on each branch so transient EHR rejections are absorbed rather than surfacing as failures.
options.C: An instruction in each subagent's prompt telling it to pace its EHR calls and avoid bursts during ward rounds.
options.D: A shared rate limiter in front of the EHR from which any branch must take a permit before calling.
options.E: A move to a cheaper model tier for the branches, reducing the system's overall resource consumption.

items.question: An academic publisher runs a drafting agent and a reviewing agent that exchange revisions of a book blurb. Most titles settle in two or three rounds. A minority run past thirty rounds, with the reviewer requesting ever-smaller wording changes, and cost per title is unpredictable enough that finance has flagged it. The iteration genuinely improves early rounds. What should be added?

options.A: Instruct the reviewer to apply a stricter acceptance standard, so it sends fewer drafts back and most titles settle sooner.
options.B: Move the drafting agent to a higher-capability tier so its first draft needs fewer revision rounds before acceptance.
options.C: Cap the rounds, require an explicit accept-or-revise decision each round, stop below a materiality threshold, and escalate to an editor at the cap.
options.D: Have the reviewer comment once on the final draft rather than iterating, converting the exchange into a single review step before publication.

items.question: What should the default be for state in a multi-agent system, before any specific requirement is considered?

options.A: Private to each agent, with anything shared introduced deliberately as a defined, versioned artefact where a contract requires it.
options.B: Shared across all agents, so every agent works from a consistent view and no information is duplicated.
options.C: Shared and readable by all agents but writable only by the orchestrator, giving consistency without write conflicts.
options.D: Held entirely in the orchestrator's conversation, with agents receiving whatever slice they need at invocation.

items.question: An energy retailer's tariff-comparison assistant fans out to six subagents, each of which calls a legacy pricing service. That service serialises all requests for a given customer account and takes roughly three seconds per call, so the six branches complete in about eighteen seconds regardless of how they are scheduled. A proposal on the table is to split into twelve branches to increase parallelism. What should the team do next?

options.A: Approve the split to twelve branches and re-measure end-to-end time, since more parallelism should reduce the wall clock.
options.B: Leave the topology alone and address the pricing service — batch the six lookups into one call, or pre-materialise the tariffs.
options.C: Keep six branches but move them to a faster model tier so the non-pricing portion of each branch completes about a second sooner.
options.D: Raise the request deadline from fifteen to twenty-five seconds so the current design fits inside it reliably.

items.question: A telematics company's multi-agent claims-triage system has become steadily more expensive per request over two quarters, while traffic and task difficulty have been flat. The team wants standing metrics that would reveal coordination overhead growing, early, rather than at quarterly review. Which TWO metrics best serve that purpose? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: End-to-end p95 latency for the request, from intake to the answer shown to the adjuster.
options.B: The distribution of delegation depth and branch count per triage request, tracked week over week.
options.C: Tool error rate for each integrated tool, broken down by error class and originating branch.
options.D: Mean length of the final triage answer returned to the adjuster on each completed request.
options.E: The share of request tokens spent establishing subagent context and ingesting returns, rather than on the task.

items.question: A recruitment platform piloted a five-branch multi-agent design against its existing single-agent baseline for candidate–role matching. The multi-agent version costs roughly five times as much per request and scores three points higher on the team's matching-quality metric. Product wants to ship it; the platform lead wants the spend defended. Neither has data on which branches contribute what. What should be done next?

options.A: Ship the multi-agent version now and optimise its per-request cost once adoption data is available.
options.B: Revert to the single-agent baseline, since a three-point quality gain does not justify a fivefold increase in cost per request.
options.C: Move all five branches to a cheaper model tier and re-measure both matching quality and cost per request.
options.D: Run an ablation, measuring quality with each branch removed in turn, so the gain can be attributed per branch.

items.question: A customs brokerage dispatches subagent tasks onto a message queue and collects results asynchronously. Last month a branch failed permanently, its message was routed to the dead-letter queue after redelivery, and no result ever came back. The orchestrator waited indefinitely; the shipment request sat unresolved for two days until a client called. What should the design add?

options.A: A per-request ledger of every dispatched branch, with a deadline after which an unresolved branch is failed and the partial-failure policy applies.
options.B: An alert on dead-letter queue depth so the on-call operator is paged whenever a branch's message is parked there.
options.C: A longer message visibility timeout and more redelivery attempts, so a branch is less likely to be declared permanently failed.
options.D: Automatic replay of dead-lettered branch messages back onto the main queue on a fifteen-minute schedule.

items.question: A museum's cataloguing assistant drafts object descriptions in a long conversation with a curator. The team added a tone-check subagent, but to judge tone it needs the full drafted description and the whole preceding conversation about the object, all of which the orchestrator forwards on every call. Cost rose and nothing improved. What should the team do?

options.A: Forward a summary of the conversation instead of the full history to reduce the tokens sent to the subagent.
options.B: Give the tone-check subagent a larger context allowance so forwarding the full history is less constrained.
options.C: Perform the tone check inline in the drafting agent, which already holds everything the check requires.
options.D: Run the tone check on the finished description alone, with none of the curator conversation attached.

items.question: A football club's recruitment system fans out to four scouting subagents that run concurrently. One of them normalises its player ratings against a positional benchmark that another branch computes and writes to the shared store during the same run. Because both start together, the normalising branch reads whichever benchmark is already there — usually the previous run's. Shortlists have been produced against stale benchmarks for weeks with no error raised. What should the architect change?

options.A: Have the normalising branch poll the shared store until the current run's benchmark appears before it starts normalising.
options.B: Compute the benchmark before the fan-out and carry its value in the handoff to every branch that needs it.
options.C: Version the benchmark with the run identifier so the normalising branch can detect when what it read is from a previous run.
options.D: Run all four branches sequentially in a fixed order so that any dependency between them is always satisfied.

items.question: A platform team hosts twenty specialist agents used by several product orchestrators. Each agent is described by a one-line prose summary, and orchestrators choose between them by reading those summaries. Product teams report invocations that fail deep inside a branch because the agent required an input the caller did not have, and two agents whose summaries read almost identically are picked interchangeably despite very different cost and tool scope. What should the platform team publish instead?

options.A: A machine-readable capability contract per agent — schemas, preconditions, tool scope and cost class — checked at the boundary.
options.B: Longer and more carefully written prose descriptions spelling out each agent's inputs, limitations, cost and typical use cases.
options.C: A convention that orchestrators attempt the cheapest plausible agent first and fall back to the next one when that attempt fails.
options.D: A consolidation of the twenty agents into five broader ones, removing most of the choices a calling orchestrator has to make.

items.question: Why should a subagent invocation be designed to carry no state from previous invocations of the same agent?

options.A: Because a stateful agent's growing history would be replayed into the orchestrator's context window on every one of its later calls.
options.B: Because state carried between invocations cannot be serialised into a structured schema the caller is able to inspect.
options.C: Because an agent that holds state between calls cannot be given a tool allowlist narrower than its caller's.
options.D: Because a stateless invocation is a pure function of its brief, so it can be retried, parallelised and replayed reproducibly.

items.question: A rail operator's disruption-compensation system fans out to several subagents, one of which can issue refunds. During a major incident the orchestrator hit its per-branch deadline, treated the refund branch as failed, degraded gracefully and told the passenger a manual review would follow. Ninety seconds later the abandoned branch completed and issued the refund anyway; some passengers were then refunded twice by the manual process. What must the design add?

options.A: A longer deadline on the refund branch specifically, so that slow refunds complete before the orchestrator gives up on it.
options.B: Cancellation propagated to the branch on deadline, plus a fencing token so the refund tool rejects a write from an abandoned branch.
options.C: A nightly reconciliation job that detects duplicate refunds after the fact and reverses the second payment to the passenger.
options.D: A rule that the manual review process must wait until every dispatched branch has finished or timed out before it begins.

items.question: A wholesale distributor's ordering assistant has three levels: orchestrator, coordinator agents, and worker agents. Each level retries a failed call three times. When one downstream inventory service degrades, a single user request can produce dozens of attempts against it, and the service's recovery is delayed by the load. Which TWO changes address the amplification? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Retry at exactly one level and have the other levels propagate a typed failure upward without attempting their own retries.
options.B: Add jitter to the backoff at every level so retries from different branches do not synchronise into bursts.
options.C: Keep retries at every level but lengthen the timeout at each, so fewer calls are declared failed in the first place.
options.D: Give the request one retry budget, decremented wherever in the tree a retry is attempted, so total attempts are bounded.
options.E: Increase the retry count at the worker level so transient failures are resolved before they reach a coordinator.

items.question: A container shipping line assesses port-call risk with three subagents. One returns a numeric score from one to five, one returns a paragraph of narrative, and one returns a list of flags with no severity. The aggregator's prompt has grown into a set of special-case rules for translating each format, and adding a fourth branch has been deferred twice because of the work involved. Operations wants comparable risk across branches. What should change?

options.A: Have the aggregator convert each branch's output into a common form as its first step, leaving the three branches unchanged.
options.B: Rank the three branches by historical reliability and let the most reliable branch's format define the result for all of them.
options.C: Define one return contract every branch must satisfy — a severity on a shared scale, a rationale and evidence references.
options.D: Drop the narrative branch, since a paragraph of prose cannot be compared against a numeric score or a list of flags.

items.question: A facilities-management firm runs a nightly compliance sweep with one subagent per site across 400 sites. Each branch returns a structured finding capped at roughly 800 tokens, so the full set is far more than one aggregation call can hold. The aggregate must state, for every site, whether it passed, and must not silently omit any site. Currently the aggregator is fed as many returns as fit and the rest are dropped. What should the design do?

options.A: Aggregate in tiers — 20 groups of 20 into the same schema, then the 20 group results — carrying site counts at every level.
options.B: Move the aggregation to a model with the largest available context window and feed it all 400 site returns in a single call.
options.C: Sample 50 sites each night for aggregation and rotate the sample, so the whole estate is covered over a period of weeks.
options.D: Reduce each branch's return to a single pass or fail token so that all 400 fit inside one aggregation call.

items.question: An orchestrator's only behaviour is to call one subagent and return its output unchanged, and no further branches are planned. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep the orchestrator so that additional branches can be added later without restructuring the call path or its clients.
options.B: Keep the orchestrator because it is where the subagent's output schema is validated before returning.
options.C: Keep the orchestrator because it is where the request's correlation id and tracing spans are attached.
options.D: Remove the orchestrator and call the agent directly, since the layer isolates nothing and decides nothing.

items.question: A national statistics office splits its survey-methodology review into four subagents. The split was introduced eighteen months ago because a single agent lost track of the review checklist once the questionnaire and prior-wave documentation were loaded together. The team has now migrated to a substantially more capable model and is planning further work on the orchestration layer, including a new aggregation contract. What should they do first?

options.A: Proceed with the planned orchestration work, since the split has been stable in production for eighteen months.
options.B: Re-run the single-agent baseline on the current eval set with the new model, to see whether the original constraint still binds.
options.C: Add a fifth subagent to cover the new documentation types introduced since the original four-way design.
options.D: Move the four subagents to a cheaper tier now that the orchestrator is stronger, and measure the cost saving.

items.question: Which THREE properties should an inter-agent error contract have so that a caller can act on a failure without inspecting it manually? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Every failure maps to one generic error type, so callers have a single, simple handling path.
options.B: Every failure is classified as either retryable or terminal by the agent that observed it.
options.C: Each error class states the expected caller response — retry, degrade, or abort the request.
options.D: The failing agent's full transcript is attached to the error so the caller can diagnose the cause.
options.E: The error carries a correlation id that resolves to the full detail in logs, rather than the detail itself.

items.question: A media-monitoring firm's brand-sentiment agent runs a refinement loop: on each iteration it fans out to eight source subagents, reads their returns, refines its interpretation, and iterates. Typical runs take four to six iterations. Review of the traces shows each iteration sends the eight branches a slightly reworded brief and receives substantively the same material back, because the underlying sources do not change during a run. Cost per report is roughly five times the original estimate. What should change?

options.A: Fan out once at the start and run the refinement loop over the eight returns without re-invoking the branches.
options.B: Move the eight source subagents to the cheapest available tier, since they only gather material rather than reason over it.
options.C: Cap the refinement loop at three iterations, bounding the number of fan-outs performed for each sentiment report.
options.D: Cache each branch's return keyed on the brief text, so repeated invocations within a run are served from the cache.

items.question: An accountancy firm's advisory assistant has grown to fourteen specialist subagents. Nine of them are invoked on fewer than one per cent of requests, yet each carries a prompt to maintain, an evaluation set to keep current, a version to track and a monitoring dashboard. Quality on the rare paths is unmeasured because the volume is too low to score. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep all fourteen, since removing any specialist would reduce the assistant's coverage of the unusual requests it handles.
options.B: Keep the nine rare specialists but move them to the cheapest available tier, since they handle so little traffic.
options.C: Fold the rare specialists into one general agent with their tools, keeping separate agents only where volume supports them.
options.D: Generate the nine rare agents' prompts automatically from a shared template so each one costs far less to maintain.

items.question: A broadband provider added a customer-history subagent that keeps a persistent memory so it can recall context between calls. Support staff have begun seeing it reference another customer's outage history and, on one occasion, another customer's address, because the memory accumulates across every request the agent serves. The recall of prior interactions is genuinely valuable to agents handling repeat callers. How should this be redesigned?

options.A: Partition the agent's persistent memory by customer and instruct it to read only the partition matching the current caller.
options.B: Clear the agent's persistent memory on a nightly schedule so accumulated context cannot grow large enough to leak.
options.C: Run a separate long-lived instance of the agent for each customer, each holding only that customer's memory.
options.D: Keep the agent stateless and hold history in a store keyed by customer, retrieved into the brief for each request.

items.question: A genomics laboratory's variant-interpretation system runs under a fixed per-request budget. The budget affords either eight branches doing a shallow pass over eight genomic regions, or three branches doing a thorough pass over three. Currently it runs eight shallow. A review of 120 failed interpretations found 96 were incorrect conclusions about regions the system had examined, and 24 concerned regions it never looked at. Which change does the evidence support?

options.A: Keep eight branches and cut the per-branch budget further so a ninth and tenth genomic region can be added.
options.B: Keep eight branches and add a verification agent over the aggregate interpretation, funded from the same fixed budget.
options.C: Move to three thorough branches on the regions with the highest clinical yield, since most failures come from insufficient depth.
options.D: Keep eight branches and escalate to a human curator whenever any one of them reports low confidence in its call.

items.question: Quality has fallen in a fan-out-and-synthesise design, and the team must decide whether to invest in the branches or in the aggregation step. Which TWO observations would indicate the aggregation step is the source of the loss? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Branch outputs each score as correct when reviewed individually, yet the final answer contradicts them.
options.B: Branches frequently return typed error results to the aggregator rather than findings.
options.C: Aggregate latency on most requests is dominated by the single slowest branch in the fan-out.
options.D: Replaying a stored set of branch outputs through the aggregator gives materially different answers on different runs.
options.E: Branch outputs regularly exceed the size budget set out in their own return contract.

items.question: A wholesaler's ERP data-cleansing system runs branches in parallel over customer records. In a postmortem, two branches — one deduplicating and one standardising addresses — both amended the same customer record within the same second, in incompatible ways. The last write won, the other change was lost, and the audit trail shows two conflicting amendments with no indication which was intended. The parallelism is needed to finish the nightly window. What should the team do next?

options.A: Partition write ownership so one branch owns each record, with other branches emitting proposals for it to apply.
options.B: Take a row-level lock on each customer record for the duration of the amendment a branch is making.
options.C: Add optimistic concurrency control so the second writer detects the conflicting version and retries against the updated record.
options.D: Order the branches so that deduplication always runs before address standardisation across the whole nightly job.

items.question: A mortgage servicer's hardship-review system uses four subagents to read bank statements, correspondence, arrears history and affordability models, each returning a structured assessment. Because an early pilot produced two poor recommendations, the orchestrator was changed to re-read all four underlying document sets itself before deciding. Cost per review roughly doubled, latency rose, and the orchestrator now hits context pressure on large cases. Recommendation quality is unchanged. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep the re-reading but restrict it to the two document sets implicated in the two original poor recommendations.
options.B: Remove the wholesale re-reading and rely on branch assessments, with a code-level consistency check and sampled spot-checks.
options.C: Keep the re-reading and move the orchestrator to a model with far more context headroom to relieve the pressure on large cases.
options.D: Remove the re-reading and add a fifth reviewing agent that repeats the four assessments independently and compares the results.

items.question: A team is drawing the responsibility boundary between its orchestrator and its specialist subagents. Which TWO responsibilities must sit with the orchestrator rather than being pushed into the branches? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The domain reasoning that is specific to each specialist's subject area.
options.B: The request-level budget and deadline all branches must collectively operate inside.
options.C: The decision about which branches to invoke for a given incoming request.
options.D: The credentials used to reach the underlying data source behind each specialist.
options.E: Retrying a branch's own internal tool call after a transient network error.

items.question: A postal operator handles parcel exceptions with a five-agent investigation flow that queries three back-end systems. It meets its quality bar but averages nine seconds against a five-second SLO for the agent-facing console, and unit cost is under pressure at volume. Analysis of a month of traffic shows 60% of exceptions are one of four routine types resolvable from a single system lookup, and the remaining 40% genuinely require correlating all three systems. What is the strongest architecture?

options.A: Keep the five-agent flow for all traffic and negotiate the console SLO up to ten seconds on the basis of the quality it delivers.
options.B: Keep the five-agent flow for all traffic and move every agent to the fastest available tier to bring the average within the SLO.
options.C: Replace the five-agent flow entirely with a single agent holding all three system tools, accepting some quality loss on complex exceptions.
options.D: Resolve the four routine types inline with a single agent and one lookup, routing only the complex 40% into the multi-agent flow.

items.question: For a single Claude request with a large prompt and a moderate-length response, which factor most directly drives total wall-clock latency?

options.A: Output token count, because generation proceeds one token at a time, so response length sets most of the wall clock.
options.B: Input token count, because every input token must be decoded one at a time before the first output token can be produced.
options.C: Network round-trip time and TLS handshake setup between the calling service and the regional API endpoint.
options.D: The number of tool definitions in the request, each of which is validated in sequence before generation starts.

items.question: A freight brokerage exposes a shipment-exception triage endpoint to its carrier partners under a 2,000 ms p95 contractual budget. Measured end-to-end p95 today is 1,780 ms, leaving 220 ms of headroom. The mean stage breakdown from tracing is: auth and routing 20 ms, retrieval from the exceptions index 120 ms, a single Sonnet-tier call 960 ms, response shaping 40 ms, egress 40 ms. Product now wants the exception classified into one of 40 categories *before* retrieval, so retrieval can be filtered by category. The prototype classifier is a second model call on the same tier that emits a short justification plus the label, and it measures 500 ms p95 and 320 ms mean. Adding it serially puts the endpoint over budget. What is the best design response?

options.A: Re-implement the classifier on the fastest tier, capped at a single label token with no justification, then re-measure against the 220 ms of headroom.
options.B: Cache the classification in the existing Redis layer keyed on shipment id, so most exception events find a warm entry and skip the classifier call.
options.C: Issue the classifier call concurrently with retrieval so the two stages overlap, discarding the retrieval result whenever the returned category does not match.
options.D: Convert the endpoint to an accepted-then-callback contract with a webhook per carrier partner, so the p95 budget covers only the acknowledgement.

items.question: A pharmacy benefit manager is reviewing a prior-authorisation assistant against a 2,000 ms p95 budget. The team's design document adds the measured p95 of each non-overlapping trace span — request validation 90 ms, member and formulary retrieval 260 ms, the model call 1,820 ms, response assembly 140 ms — for a total of 2,310 ms, and concludes the design cannot meet the budget. A shadow deployment carrying mirrored production traffic reports a measured end-to-end p95 of 1,690 ms. The spans do not overlap and the clocks are synchronised. Which reading of this is correct?

options.A: The shadow figure is optimistic because mirrored traffic under-represents the real request mix; the additive 2,310 ms estimate should be treated as the planning number.
options.B: The discrepancy indicates instrumentation loss in the model-call span; the team should re-instrument and re-derive the budget from the corrected stage sum.
options.C: Both figures are valid for different purposes: the sum is the true p95 and the shadow figure is the p50, so the design meets the budget only half the time.
options.D: Percentiles are not additive: 2,310 ms is a request at the tail of every stage at once, which is rare. The measured end-to-end p95 is the real number.

items.question: A service must sustain 40 requests per second with a mean end-to-end latency of 3 seconds. Approximately what in-flight concurrency must the calling tier support?

options.A: Roughly 13 concurrent requests.
options.B: About 40 concurrent requests.
options.C: About 120 concurrent requests.
options.D: Roughly 400 concurrent requests.

items.question: A specialty retailer runs a Claude-backed customer service assistant. Thirty days of traffic analysis shows: 72% of question texts are unique within the window; the 300 most frequent questions together account for 9% of volume; and every response is personalised with the customer's order history, loyalty status and open returns before it is sent. Finance has asked for a caching strategy to cut spend. Which TWO statements are supported by this distribution? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: An exact-match response cache keyed only on the question text is unsafe here, because stored responses embed one customer's order and returns data.
options.B: Caching the retrieved product, policy and shipping documents is shareable across customers, because the retrieved corpus is not personalised even though the response is.
options.C: The 300 most frequent questions make a response cache the highest-leverage change available, because head-of-distribution traffic is where response caching always pays.
options.D: A semantic cache over question embeddings, with the similarity threshold loosened, will lift the effective hit rate above 70% given the observed query variety.
options.E: Because 72% of question texts are unique within the window, no caching layer — response, semantic or document — can meaningfully reduce spend on this workload.

items.question: A commercial insurer triages first-notice-of-loss submissions with a cascade: a Haiku-tier first pass at a measured $0.0008 per call handles the submission, and low-confidence cases escalate to an Opus-tier adjudication at a measured $0.019 per call. At launch, 25% escalated. Since a new marine cargo product went live, the escalation rate has settled at 58%. Finance has flagged the cost line and asked whether the cascade should be abandoned in favour of sending everything to the Opus tier. Which characterisation of the drift is accurate?

options.A: The cascade has crossed over: at 58% escalation the cheap first pass is pure overhead on top of an adjudication that happens anyway, so routing everything straight to the Opus tier costs less.
options.B: Blended cost per submission has more than doubled, but the cascade still runs roughly 38% below flat Opus-tier routing and break-even sits near a 96% escalation rate; the regression is latency, not cost.
options.C: Cost per submission is essentially unchanged, because the Haiku-tier first pass is negligible next to the adjudication call and only the escalated share ever moved the line.
options.D: The cascade saves the same proportion it always did, because both tiers price linearly per submission and the ratio between the first-pass and adjudication rates is fixed.

items.question: An online games publisher runs player-report moderation on Claude. During a tournament weekend, queue depth grew from seconds to eleven minutes and p95 latency tripled. The on-call engineer doubled the worker pod count; queue depth kept growing and pod CPU sat at 28%. Telemetry shows the account's provisioned throughput allocation saturated for the whole window, with the nightly bulk re-scoring job running against the same allocation. What should the team do next?

options.A: Double the pod count again and raise the autoscaler's maximum replica ceiling, since queue depth is still growing and the current replica ceiling is what caps the drain rate.
options.B: Move the worker pods to a memory-optimised instance type so each pod can hold more in-flight requests without the connection pool thrashing under load.
options.C: Treat the throughput allocation as the binding constraint: cut tokens per request and gate the bulk job behind admission control that yields to interactive traffic.
options.D: Add a read replica for the moderation history store and warm its cache, shortening the retrieval stage that runs before every moderation call.

items.question: An architect is defining the unit-economics metric for a customer-support deflection system that will be reviewed monthly by the business. Which denominator makes the number decision-useful?

options.A: Per API call, because it reconciles one-to-one against the vendor's monthly invoice lines.
options.B: Per thousand tokens, because tokens are the unit the cost is actually incurred in.
options.C: Per resolved conversation, counting every turn, retry and failed attempt.
options.D: Per deployed environment per month, because that is the granularity of the budget.

items.question: A national benefits agency is planning capacity for an eligibility-explanation service ahead of the annual open-enrolment period. Modelling from last year gives 864,000 requests per day, with the busiest hour carrying 25% of daily volume. Mean end-to-end latency is 2.5 seconds. About a third of daily volume is a back-office caseworker batch that has no user waiting on it. Which THREE statements follow from these figures? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Sustaining the busy hour requires roughly 150 requests in flight concurrently across the worker tier at the measured mean latency.
options.B: Provisioning to the daily average of 10 requests per second leaves the busy hour short by a factor of six, surfacing as queueing delay rather than as slower model calls.
options.C: Shifting the caseworker batch out of the busy hour lowers the peak capacity requirement without reducing total daily volume.
options.D: Autoscaling the worker tier on CPU utilisation will track the enrolment spike accurately, because request volume and CPU move together in this workload.
options.E: Because the daily average is 10 requests per second, a reservation sized at 10 per second meets the latency SLO provided failed requests are retried.

items.question: A legal-tech vendor extracts change-of-control clauses from commercial contracts for corporate clients. On a held-out set of 4,000 human-labelled contracts the extractor scores 94% on that clause class, using the highest-capability tier already. A new enterprise client's contract specifies 99.5% accuracy on change-of-control extraction, with penalties. The delivery lead proposes six more weeks of prompt engineering to close the gap. As architect, what do you recommend?

options.A: Run three independent extractions per contract and majority-vote the clause spans, converting the residual errors into detectable agreement failures.
options.B: Fine-tune a smaller model on the 4,000 labelled contracts, since a task-specific model trained on the client's own clause language will beat a general-purpose one.
options.C: Treat 99.5% as a system property, not a model one: score each extraction for confidence, auto-accept above threshold, and route the rest to licensed reviewers.
options.D: Expand the few-shot set with the specific failure cases from the held-out run and re-measure on that same set before committing to the contract.

items.question: A synchronous internal API returns a Claude-generated JSON object that a downstream service parses in full before it can act. What does enabling response streaming buy this particular caller?

options.A: It lets the downstream service parse each JSON field as it arrives and begin acting on the completed ones before the object closes.
options.B: Nothing material: this caller cannot act until the final token arrives, so streaming helps only human readers or incremental consumers.
options.C: It reduces total time-to-last-token, because generation itself runs faster once tokens are being delivered incrementally.
options.D: It raises throughput, because the server can admit the next request as soon as the current one begins streaming its first tokens.

items.question: A music streaming company has five product squads, each of which embeds its own copy of a shared 900-line system prompt in its service repository. A required wording change to the artist-attribution section took three weeks to land across all five repos, one squad shipped a variant with a subtly different constraint ordering, and a sixth team has just requested a copy. Which change gives the best reduction in change cost for the effort involved?

options.A: Consolidate the five services into one shared inference service so the prompt exists in exactly one deployment and one release train to change.
options.B: Add a CI lint rule to every repo that fails the build whenever its prompt file diverges from the designated reference copy.
options.C: Publish the prompt as a versioned artefact, have each service pin a version, and gate publishes on a shared eval suite.
options.D: Move the prompt into a runtime configuration service so all five services pick up wording changes on the next request without a deploy.

items.question: A travel booking platform has added an exact-match response cache in front of its itinerary-summary endpoint. Measurements over a week: 40% hit rate, 15 ms on a hit, and the cache-miss path unchanged at 2,400 ms p95. The performance lead's summary to the steering group states that the cache "cuts p95 latency by 40%." You are asked to review the claim before it is circulated. What is the accurate correction?

options.A: With a 40% hit rate the blended p95 lands near the 92nd percentile of the miss distribution, so the tail barely moves; the real wins are mean latency and spend.
options.B: The claim is roughly right — blended p95 falls to about 1,440 ms, since 40% of requests now return in 15 ms and the reported percentile shifts in proportion.
options.C: The steering group should be shown p50 rather than p95, because the median is what most users experience and it reflects the cache benefit honestly.
options.D: The measurement is invalid: cache hits should be excluded from the latency SLO, since they bypass the model path the SLO was written to govern.

items.question: An education technology company reviews its monthly Claude spend. Spend rose 3.1x month over month; request count rose 1.15x over the same period, implying cost per request grew roughly 2.7x. No model tier change was deployed, and no pricing change was announced. Three feature teams shipped changes during the month. What should the architect do next?

options.A: Open a commercial conversation about volume-based pricing now, since spend at this level justifies a negotiated annual commitment.
options.B: Break cost per request into input and output token components by feature route, and compare the distributions against the prior month.
options.C: Move the highest-volume route to a cheaper tier behind an automated quality gate, bringing the monthly cost line back within budget this cycle.
options.D: Add an exact-match response cache to the highest-volume route, since caching is the fastest available reduction in per-request spend.

items.question: An architect is deciding whether to build an internal LLM gateway or license a vendor product that covers routing, cost attribution, key management and logging. Which factor most legitimately favours building?

options.A: The engineering team estimates it can ship a working version within one quarter of dedicated work.
options.B: The vendor's annual licence fee exceeds the estimated engineering cost of building the first release.
options.C: The vendor product is closed source, so the team cannot inspect how requests are routed and logged.
options.D: The routing and chargeback rules encode organisation-specific policy expected to change every few weeks.

items.question: An automotive parts distributor runs a four-stage document pipeline: a Haiku-tier stage extracts fields from supplier invoices, a Sonnet-tier stage reconciles them against purchase orders, and an Opus-tier stage adjudicates exceptions. The mix was chosen deliberately and the cost saving against an all-Opus design is real and measured. Which TWO recurring costs must the design budget for as a direct consequence of mixing tiers? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Every change to a shared instruction must be authored, tested and validated per tier, because identical wording does not produce identical behaviour across tiers.
options.B: A model version deprecation or upgrade becomes three independent migrations with three separate eval runs and sign-offs, rather than one.
options.C: Mixing tiers within one pipeline requires separate API credentials and a separate billing account per tier for calls to be routed correctly.
options.D: Running three tiers triples the request volume charged against the account's throughput allocation relative to a single-tier design of the same pipeline.
options.E: Because the tiers differ in capability, no stage can share an output schema with a stage running on a different tier, so each needs its own contract.

items.question: A maritime shipping line runs a customs-documentation agent that averages 10 tool-calling turns per case, resending the full transcript on each turn. Each turn adds roughly 1,500 tokens of tool output and assistant text. Finance modelled the cost as turns multiplied by average turn size — 10 x 1,500 = 15,000 input tokens per case — and the actual figure came in near 82,500, over five times the estimate. The team must now produce a capacity and cost model for next year, when volume triples. Which statement about the corrected model is right?

options.A: Cost scales linearly with turn count; the model simply used the wrong average turn size and should be recalibrated against the measured per-case figure before next year's volume triples.
options.B: Cumulative input grows roughly with the square of turn count when the whole transcript is resent, so the model must be driven by the turn-count distribution and its tail, not the mean.
options.C: Output tokens dominate agent cost in practice, so transcript growth on the input side is a second-order effect and the original model is close enough for capacity planning.
options.D: Each turn is a separate request billed independently, so per-request cost is constant and total case cost is the turn count multiplied by the cost of the first turn.

items.question: A global hotel group runs a guest-facing concierge assistant alongside a bulk job that re-summarises 400,000 property reviews. The group operates in every time zone, so there is no hour without material guest traffic. While the bulk job runs, guest-facing p95 rises from 1.4 s to 9 s. Both workloads share one worker pool and one throughput allocation. Which design change addresses this correctly?

options.A: Reschedule the bulk job to the group's lowest-traffic window and split it into smaller nightly increments per region.
options.B: Raise the client timeout on the guest path from 5 s to 12 s so the elevated p95 stops surfacing to guests as errors.
options.C: Scale the shared worker pool up for the duration of the bulk window so both workloads have enough workers to drain their queues.
options.D: Give the bulk job its own lane with capped concurrency and admission control that yields to interactive traffic.

items.question: When an architect builds a cost-at-volume model for a Claude-based feature, which component is most commonly omitted altogether?

options.A: Tokens consumed by work that never reaches a user: retries, timed-out calls, and outputs rejected by validation.
options.B: Input tokens, which are frequently counted only for the user's message and never for the retrieved context passages.
options.C: The system prompt and few-shot examples, which are re-sent in full on every single request.
options.D: The hosting and index-refresh cost of the vector database backing document retrieval.

items.question: A telecommunications operator runs an agent-assist system in its contact centre. When an advisor sends a message, the platform must return a suggested reply within a 900 ms p95 budget or advisors stop using it. The product team also wants each interaction enriched with sentiment scoring, a coaching note for the advisor's supervisor and a taxonomy label for reporting. None of those three outputs is shown to the advisor during the call; they appear in a supervisor dashboard and in next-day reporting. Prototypes put the enrichment at 1,400 ms. What is the right architecture?

options.A: Run the enrichment concurrently with the suggested-reply call and return once both complete, so the two do not add serially.
options.B: Publish the interaction to an event stream keyed by conversation id and run the three enrichments as downstream consumers; the interactive path returns only the reply.
options.C: Move the enrichment to the cheapest tier and cap its output tightly so all three outputs fit inside the 900 ms budget alongside the reply.
options.D: Return the suggested reply immediately and have the advisor's client poll a second endpoint for the enrichment results as they land.

items.question: A pharmaceutical distributor runs an order-exception assistant sized for 25 requests per second. The calling tier has a hard concurrency cap of 120 in-flight requests, and at design load mean end-to-end latency is 4 seconds. During a supplier recall, order histories grew much longer, and mean latency rose to 10 seconds. Completed throughput fell to roughly 12 requests per second and the backlog grew continuously. The account's provisioned throughput allocation was at 45% utilisation throughout, and worker CPU never exceeded 30%. What explains the collapse?

options.A: The upstream throughput allocation became the binding constraint once payload sizes grew, throttling token delivery and holding completions to roughly half the design rate for the whole recall.
options.B: With concurrency capped at 120, completed throughput is the cap divided by mean latency — 30 per second at 4 seconds, 12 per second at 10 seconds — so the pool itself became the limiter.
options.C: Retries of backlogged requests amplified offered load beyond what the system could absorb, and that amplification alone accounts for the drop in completions.
options.D: The design used mean latency where it should have used p95; correcting the sizing calculation to the p95 figure explains the observed 12 per second.

items.question: A veterinary telehealth platform is evaluating a semantic cache in front of its triage-advice assistant, matching an incoming question against stored question embeddings and returning the stored answer above a similarity threshold. Traffic is high volume, the advice is derived from a clinical guidance corpus that is revised several times a year, and the assistant already passes its accuracy evaluation. Which THREE statements about this design are correct? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The similarity threshold is a direct trade of hit rate against the risk of answering a materially different question, so it must be tuned on an evaluation set of near-miss pairs.
options.B: Cache entries must be invalidated when the clinical guidance corpus is revised, or the cache will continue serving superseded advice indefinitely after the source has changed.
options.C: Negations and small numeric differences — a dose for a 4 kg cat versus a 40 kg dog — can sit close together in embedding space while being clinically opposite, so proximity is not equivalence.
options.D: A semantic cache removes the need to evaluate cached responses, because every stored answer passed the accuracy evaluation at the moment it was first generated.
options.E: Because embedding generation is deterministic and the threshold is fixed, a semantic cache introduces no failure modes beyond those already present in an exact-match cache.

items.question: An agricultural commodities trader runs a five-stage extraction chain over shipping and quality documents: parse, normalise units, match to contract, compute tolerance breaches, and draft the counterparty notice. Each stage is evaluated in isolation against its own reference set and each scores 97%. The team's design document reports the system as "97% accurate". An end-to-end evaluation on 1,200 complete cases returns 86%. What is the correct interpretation?

options.A: The end-to-end reference set is materially harder than the per-stage sets, and the two figures should be reconciled by re-sampling the end-to-end set to match the stage distributions.
options.B: One stage is likely regressing under real inputs; the 11-point gap should be localised by comparing per-stage scores on the end-to-end set before any design change is made.
options.C: In a serial chain where a stage's error is not recoverable downstream, stage accuracies multiply: 0.97 to the fifth power is about 86%, which matches the measurement.
options.D: Errors partially cancel across stages, so end-to-end accuracy should exceed the weakest stage; 86% indicates a defect in how the end-to-end evaluation grades partial credit.

items.question: A design can either produce a 2,000-token report in one call, or split it into five independent 400-token sections generated concurrently and joined by a short assembly call. Which is the better latency bet and why?

options.A: The single call, because five concurrent calls multiply connection setup and per-request overhead beyond any saving from shorter generation.
options.B: They are equivalent, because the same total number of output tokens must be produced either way, so the same generation time is spent.
options.C: The single call, because the assembly step must wait for all five sections to finish before it can start, and therefore reintroduces the full serial cost.
options.D: The parallel design, because generation is sequential per call, so wall time tracks the longest single output — about 400 tokens plus assembly — not all 2,000.

items.question: A recruitment SaaS company runs a multi-turn interview-preparation agent. Each session's transcript and tool results are held in the serving pod's memory and keyed by session id. Two problems have appeared: load across pods is badly uneven because long sessions pin users to one pod, and every scale-in event or pod restart destroys the sessions on that pod, which users experience as the agent forgetting everything. Traffic is growing 20% a month. Which change addresses both problems?

options.A: Externalise session state to a shared store keyed by session id, so any pod can serve any turn.
options.B: Introduce consistent-hash sticky routing on session id so every turn reliably reaches the pod holding that session.
options.C: Extend the pod termination grace period so in-flight sessions can complete before a pod is removed during scale-in.
options.D: Disable scale-in during business hours and scale only upward until the evening traffic trough arrives.

items.question: An energy utility is deciding between licensing a document-intelligence platform and building the equivalent in-house. The vendor quote is $480,000 per year, excluding inference spend. The internal estimate is $600,000 one-off to reach feature parity, then $250,000 per year to run, also excluding inference spend, which the finance team confirms is the same under either option. A director has circulated a note saying the build "pays for itself in fifteen months". Which TWO observations should most influence the decision? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Payback is closer to 2.6 years: the build saves $230,000 a year against the licence, and $600,000 divided by $230,000 is about 2.6 — long relative to how fast the tooling shifts.
options.B: The $250,000 annual run estimate warrants more scrutiny than the $600,000 build estimate, because payback is far more sensitive to an error in the recurring figure than in the one-off.
options.C: Because the build is cheaper from year three onward, the decision resolves itself as soon as the planning horizon is set beyond three years, and no further analysis is needed.
options.D: Exit cost from the vendor should be excluded from the comparison, since it is incurred only if the buy decision is later reversed and is not a year-one cash item.
options.E: The director's fifteen-month figure is defensible, since the annual licence of $480,000 covers most of the $600,000 build cost within about fifteen months of avoided fees.
